doc.title: Ellen Rowe interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 2, 2024

title: Transcribing from records and tape, Marian McPartland's Dudley Moore portrait
summary: Both recall learning by repeatedly replaying; Rowe transcribed a McPartland piece from a sharp-running tape, and argues transcribing yourself honors the roots.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: It’s very interesting how, you mentioned deep listening and how connected it is to technology. Because I was reading your bio and it reminded me of how I used to learn songs from records. So you know I want to learn the bass line first and there was this constant putting the needle down, getting a couple of measures, picking the needle up. I mean that was deep. Because you had no choice, it was deep.
Exactly. Yeah. I remember like cassette recordings I had of Marian McPartland when I was trying to transcribe her solo piano albums and you know it was push and rewind and © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

push and rewind and push and rewind. And you know the other beauty about that was that — one tape I remember in particular was running almost a half-step sharp and I transcribed a solo piece for — it was, she used to do these portraits of her guests sometimes on the Piano Jazz show. And she did a portrait of Dudley Moore. And I painstakingly took that sucker down. I could not believe she had played in C sharp minor but you know she was Marian, she could play in any key. And sure enough she goes, “I could never play this” or whatever it was, and yeah, she had played it in C minor. But that was a lesson to myself to somehow find a way to check those. But yeah, and I got off track here because I had something else I was planning to say. Oh yeah, the drop the needle — yeah I mean I almost kind of say that, and especially in my jazz pedagogy classes I say that jazz pedagogy is a double edged sword because we have all these technical wonders at our disposal, we have all the streaming sites which of course I have very mixed feelings about as do any other composers and performers who are not getting any royalties. But there’s how-to books and how-to videos and there’s all types of pre- transcribed solos out there that people can use, and etude books. And you know I mean I think they’re all out there, being put out there by very well meaning people but the you know I think we both agree that the way you really get at the essence of what’s going on is to do this deep listening and to teach yourself, you know do the transcribing yourself, not play somebody’s transcription that’s already out there. So I mean I think we need to honor the roots of the music by doing as much work by ear as we can and take advantage of the pedagogical benefits I guess, if that’s the right word, of having all this material at our disposal. But you know I think about the way all the great masters learned. You know they didn’t have Aebersold play-a-longs and etude books and pre-transcribed solos and things like that. And I would argue that their method of learning created the masters that they are. So yeah. I could go on and on about this but —
